---
title: "7 Waves"
subtitle: "Progressive waves, transverse and longitudinal waves, the Doppler effect, the electromagnetic spectrum and polarisation"
---

## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- describe wave motion as illustrated by vibration in ropes, springs and ripple tanks;
- use the terms displacement, amplitude, phase difference, period, frequency, wavelength and speed;
- use the time-base and y-gain of a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) to determine frequency and amplitude;
- derive and use the wave equation $v=f\lambda$;
- understand that energy is transferred by a progressive wave;
- recall and use intensity $=\text{power}/\text{area}$ and intensity $\propto(\text{amplitude})^2$;
- compare transverse and longitudinal waves, and interpret graphical representations of both;
- understand the Doppler effect for sound and use $f_o=f_s\dfrac{v}{v\pm v_s}$;
- state the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum and their wavelength ranges;
- understand polarisation and use Malus's law $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$.

## 7.1 Progressive waves

::: {.study-card}
### Wave motion

A **progressive wave** transfers energy from one place to another without transferring matter. Wave motion can be seen when a pulse travels along a stretched rope or spring, or across the surface of a ripple tank: each particle oscillates about a fixed position while the disturbance (the wave) moves on.

Key terms:

- **Displacement** $x$ is the distance of a particle from its equilibrium position (measured in m).
- **Amplitude** $A$ is the maximum displacement from equilibrium (m).
- **Wavelength** $\lambda$ is the distance between two successive points oscillating in phase (m).
- **Period** $T$ is the time for one complete oscillation (s).
- **Frequency** $f$ is the number of complete oscillations per second (Hz), with $f=1/T$.
- **Phase difference** is the fraction of a cycle between two points, usually measured in degrees or radians.
- **Speed** $v$ is the distance travelled by the wave per unit time.
:::

::: {.formula-panel}
### The wave equation

Since one wavelength is travelled in one period:

$$v=\frac{\lambda}{T}=f\lambda.$$

The wave equation can be derived from the definitions of speed, frequency and wavelength. It applies to all waves, including sound, light and water waves.
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Energy and intensity

A progressive wave carries energy. The **intensity** of a wave is the power transmitted per unit cross-sectional area:

$$I=\frac{P}{A}.$$

For a progressive wave, the intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude:

$$I\propto A^2.$$

Doubling the amplitude therefore quadruples the intensity.
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Using a cathode-ray oscilloscope

On a CRO, the **time-base** controls the horizontal axis (time per division) and the **y-gain** controls the vertical axis (voltage or displacement per division).

- The **period** is read from the horizontal scale: count the time for one complete cycle.
- The **amplitude** is read from the vertical scale: the height of a peak above the centre line.
- The **frequency** is then $f=1/T$.
:::

## 7.2 Transverse and longitudinal waves

::: {.study-card}
### Comparing transverse and longitudinal waves

In a **transverse wave**, the particles vibrate perpendicular (at $90^\circ$) to the direction of energy transfer. Examples: waves on a rope, water waves, electromagnetic waves.

In a **longitudinal wave**, the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer. The wave consists of compressions and rarefactions. Examples: sound waves in air, waves on a slinky spring.

Graphically, a transverse wave is drawn as a sine curve of displacement against distance; a longitudinal wave is represented by the same sinusoidal graph, where positive displacement means a compression and negative displacement a rarefaction.
:::

::: {.study-card}
### Doppler effect for sound

When a source of sound moves relative to a stationary observer, the observed frequency differs from the emitted frequency:

$$f_o=f_s\frac{v}{v\pm v_s},$$

where $v$ is the speed of sound, $v_s$ is the speed of the source and $v_o=0$ for a stationary observer.

- Source moving **towards** the observer: waves bunch up, wavelength decreases, observed frequency increases (use the minus sign).
- Source moving **away**: waves spread out, wavelength increases, observed frequency decreases (use the plus sign).
:::

## 7.3 The electromagnetic spectrum

::: {.study-card}
### Electromagnetic waves

All electromagnetic waves:

- are transverse waves;
- travel at the same speed $c=3.0\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in free space;
- transfer energy without needing a medium.

From longest wavelength to shortest wavelength, the principal regions are:

radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma-rays.

The visible region is approximately 400–700 nm.
:::

::: {.formula-panel}
### Wavelength ranges

| Region | Approximate wavelength |
|---|---|
| Radio | $>10^{-1}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| Microwaves | $10^{-1}$ – $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| Infrared | $10^{-3}$ – $7\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| Visible | $7\times10^{-7}$ – $4\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| Ultraviolet | $4\times10^{-7}$ – $10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| X-rays | $10^{-8}$ – $10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m}$ |
| Gamma-rays | $<10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m}$ |

For any region, $c=f\lambda$, so the frequency ranges are found from $\lambda=c/f$.
:::

## 7.4 Polarisation

::: {.study-card}
### Polarisation

**Polarisation** is the process by which the oscillations of a transverse wave are made to occur in one plane only. It is a property of **transverse waves only** – longitudinal waves cannot be polarised because their particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel.

An unpolarised wave vibrates in many planes perpendicular to the direction of travel. After passing through a polarising filter, the oscillations are restricted to a single plane.
:::

::: {.formula-panel}
### Malus's law

For plane-polarised light incident on a polarising filter (analyser), the transmitted intensity is

$$I=I_0\cos^2\theta,$$

where $I_0$ is the intensity of the incident polarised light and $\theta$ is the angle between the plane of polarisation of the light and the transmission axis of the filter.

When $\theta=90^\circ$, no light is transmitted; when $\theta=0^\circ$, all the light is transmitted. Note: the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ for unpolarised light passing through a first polariser is not part of Malus's law.
:::

## Chapter checklist

- [ ] I can use $v=f\lambda$ and the terms amplitude, wavelength, period, frequency and phase difference.
- [ ] I can determine frequency and amplitude from a CRO display.
- [ ] I can use intensity $=P/A$ and $I\propto A^2$.
- [ ] I can compare transverse and longitudinal waves.
- [ ] I can use the Doppler equation $f_o=f_s v/(v\pm v_s)$.
- [ ] I can name the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of wavelength.
- [ ] I can use Malus's law $I=I_0\cos^2\theta$.
